title: Issue 1 Cover — Dust on the Lens
summary: Existing approved/public-preview Issue 1 cover is the visual authority and trade-dress seed for the Sunforge Outlaw line. This RexPrompt unit records its production role without reopening or redesigning approved pixels.
settingText: Use the existing approved Issue 1 cover exactly as the cover-image authority. If the user explicitly reopens the cover for reconstruction, the story-facing promise is Brandon Mack as an ordinary drifter crossing an immense, punishing Sunfields frontier while the title tempts the reader to misread him as a fugitive.
panelPlan: Do not redesign the approved Issue 1 cover in ordinary production. Retrieve and pixel-read the actual image before any cover work.
The approved Issue 1 cover controls the line's masthead, logo/trade-dress architecture, typography character, issue-number rhythm, border/edge behavior, and recurring brand language.

If explicit reconstruction is ever requested, preserve the existing approved composition first. Story meaning should remain: ordinary Brandon against immense Sunfields scale, with enough outlaw visual grammar to make the title's false assumption plausible without depicting him as a gunslinging criminal.
No generic duel pose, no wanted-poster cliché, no false criminal backstory, no invented environmental text.

title: Issue 2 Cover — Dead Weight in the Basin
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 2, “Dead Weight in the Basin.” Sell Los Lagartos first: a visually rich itinerant brotherhood with its own hierarchy, customs and internal fault line. Brandon is compelling because this entire community looks at him and sees General Diaz.
settingText: Cinder Basin traveling camp beneath black half-buried Sunforge ribs: patchwork shade cloth, low communal tables, family tokens, route-worn gear, animal tack, water vessels, bedrolls and heat-scorched ochre ground. The camp must feel mobile, culturally specific and heavily lived in.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: Brandon has walked into a striking community already divided over authority, and both sides suddenly treat him as the absent General who can settle it.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Low-to-medium wide portrait composition from just inside the communal gathering, roughly a 35mm-feeling lens. Brandon is near center but not oversized. Two organically different clusters of Los Lagartos frame him from left and right, creating social pressure. Sand Rider occupies a strong secondary silhouette in travel gear. A practical empty place associated with Diaz may exist near the table edge, but it is not the star.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: First read: the faces and body language of Los Lagartos—hope, suspicion, deference, impatience—converging on Brandon. Second read: Brandon's restrained refusal to perform authority. Third read: Sand Rider and the competing community factions. Make individual Lagartos visibly distinct within a coherent shared culture.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: Show actual traveling-life texture: patched shade cloths, family tokens, layered dust-dark coats, repairs, communal food, water rationing hardware, route markers without readable text, children/elders or workers only if they remain subordinate to the focal hierarchy. The camp should look like a society on the move, not a military encampment.

LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Hard high basin light broken by warm dusty reflected light under patched shade. Sunforge ribs are matte black/oxidized and inert. Clothing should carry route wear, sweat, dust, leather, canvas and individual family details rather than uniformity.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: The General's place can be visible as one practical gap in the social geometry, but the real symbol is the community's collective gaze assigning Brandon a role.

THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, read as one dark-coated outsider caught between two visually distinct groups beneath black ribs. Brandon and the surrounding community must remain more legible than any empty chair or prop.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not show the later armed intervention, Brandon's argument that they must choose without Diaz, Raina questioning camp members, or the preacher clue.
MUST INCLUDE: Los Lagartos as visually compelling community; Sand Rider as a distinctive secondary figure; Brandon under collective expectation; black Sunforge ribs and mobile camp texture.
MUST AVOID: throne imagery; military uniforms; generic faceless crowd; Brandon dressed as Diaz; gunfight spectacle; mystical Sunforge effects.

title: Issue 3 Cover — A Shadow on the Glass
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 3, “A Shadow on the Glass.” Sell the Mirage Club as an alluring, socially specific refuge and Isabella as a magnetic person with real history—not just a mirror trick. Brandon's reflection sharpens the identity pressure.
settingText: Mirage Club below street level: cool shadow, worn reflective glass, layered curtains and salvaged metallic detail, small performance area, private alcoves, regular patrons and staff moving naturally. Above, brutal white Sunfields daylight burns at the stair opening.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: A refuge built around not asking real names contains a woman who sees Brandon and immediately knows exactly who she believes he is.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Vertical threshold composition from inside the club looking partly toward the bright stair. Isabella is foreground/near-midground and visually commands the frame with stillness. Brandon stands or descends in the bright-to-dark transition. A narrow reflective glass surface catches a displaced echo of Brandon. Eva and Jessie are present as observers, not equal poster poses.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: Isabella is the emotional focal point: composed performer posture cracking into recognition. Brandon is second: polite, wary, not theatrical. Eva should visibly clock the pattern; Jessie should read the room. Patrons in the background continue their own private social lives and register the rule breach unevenly rather than all staring in unison.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: Make the Mirage Club desirable as a place people chose: varied regulars, performers, workers, private conversation, weathered stagewear, drinks, layered textiles, salvaged mirrors, intimate tables, no sleazy villain-bar shorthand. Its culture should make the no-names rule feel valuable.

LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Extreme white exterior glare transitions into cool deep interior shadow with selective warm practical light on faces and metal. Reflections should be physically credible, not supernatural.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: The reflection is a secondary visual device that lets one face carry two histories. Isabella and the club's social reaction are the cover's true engine.
THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, read Isabella facing Brandon across a bright/dark threshold with a single reflection accent. The club should read as rich atmosphere, not black mush.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not show Merritt's locked room, photograph, Samuel's name, Eva's proposed lie test, or the later glass/photo coincidence.
MUST INCLUDE: Isabella as strong visual presence; Mirage Club patrons and culture; Brandon at threshold; one credible reflection; Eva/Jessie as observers.
MUST AVOID: two literal Brandons; ghost imagery; generic nightclub neon; empty-club minimalism; readable signage; revealing Merritt as true.

title: Issue 4 Cover — The Edge of the Sunfields
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 4, “The Edge of the Sunfields.” Sell Ray Silvestro. He should look so cool, specific and formidable that the reader wants to know who he is before learning why he is waiting for Brandon.
settingText: Lonely relay settlement at a multi-road crossing under vast hard sky: patched awning, neutral traveler tables, side rooms, water barrels, tack, messenger gear and a few unrelated travelers passing through.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: An ornate, cultivated gunslinger has been waiting at the edge of nowhere for Brandon under yet another name.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Three-quarter portrait composition, slightly low angle, with Ray occupying the dominant near-midground under shade. His refined long coat, red neckcloth, polished boots, decorative metalwork and precise sidearm should create immediate visual magnetism. Brandon approaches from hard light along one road, smaller but unmistakable. Eva and Jessie remain nearer Brandon or the rig, reading the situation.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: Ray is first read and gets the most graphic shape contrast; he should appear controlled, intelligent and dangerous without pointing a gun. Brandon is second read: road-worn, nonperformative. Eva and Jessie give the scene lived relational context. A couple of relay locals/travelers can register that a private appointment is unfolding in public.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: The relay must feel like a real neutral crossroads used by many kinds of people: patched shelter, practical first aid, baggage, water, riding gear, families and transient travelers. Avoid empty-stage Western minimalism.

LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Ray sits in dense cool shade with metallic accents and the red neckcloth catching controlled color; Brandon enters from bleached hard light. Dust and worn materials stay tactile and matte.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: A spare chair or table place may reinforce that Ray expected somebody, but Ray himself is the commercial hook. The audience should want to meet him.
THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, Ray's ornate silhouette dominates one side; Brandon's dark traveler silhouette approaches from the opposite bright road. Clear two-person tension without duel cliché.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not show Samuel, Raina, the bandaged child/family, Ray's cooled confrontation, or the confession explaining engineered tests.
MUST INCLUDE: Ray's ornate distinctive design; Brandon approaching; relay settlement life; Eva/Jessie contextual presence; multiple-road geography.
MUST AVOID: empty-chair-as-main-subject; gun draw; high-noon duel composition; Samuel/Raina reveal; generic cowboy styling.

title: Issue 5 Cover — The Useful Lie
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 5, “The Useful Lie.” Sell Bellweather as a grieving family community and Mary/Owen as people the reader immediately cares about. Brandon matters because his face has been inserted into their loss.
settingText: Bellweather during a three-day wake in light rain: connected family houses, covered porch tables, food carried between rooms, mourning cloth, wet dust, lantern-warm windows, relatives sheltering and working through grief.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: A grieving family is looking at Brandon as the missing son whose answer could settle a real promise to the dead.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Intimate medium-wide composition under a porch or awning. Mary is near foreground on one side, Owen on the other, both strong readable personalities rather than background litigants. Brandon stands within their family space but visibly outside its emotional geometry. Eva and Jessie sit/stand slightly behind him and witness the impossible social pressure. Other Bellweather relatives populate warm background layers.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: Mary's tired hope and Owen's defensive skepticism are the first emotional contrast. Brandon's calm refusal is the second. Eva's temptation to see a useful solution and Jessie's wariness may appear in subtle body language without spoiling dialogue.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: The wake should feel like family life continuing around grief: covered food, chairs actually occupied, relatives carrying cups, damp coats, children/elders in background if composition allows, domestic work, people speaking in small groups. This is a community, not an empty symbolic table.
LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Cool rainy exterior with warm amber interiors and porch lamps. Wet wood, cloth, skin and metal should feel tactile. Avoid funeral-black monochrome.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: One absent place or personal token can quietly imply Nathan, but Mary and Owen's faces must carry the cover.
THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, read as Brandon caught between two emotionally opposed family figures under rain-warm shelter; the surrounding family mass creates pressure.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not reveal the private Bell phrase, Samuel's uncertainty, Raina's audit, the housing resolution, or Brandon's later explanation of why the lie would be worse.
MUST INCLUDE: Mary and Owen as strong distinct people; Bellweather wake community; Brandon inside but not belonging to the family grouping; rain versus warm domestic light.
MUST AVOID: empty place as dominant subject; funeral body; ghost symbolism; Brandon pretending to be Nathan; reconciliation tableau; generic mourning poster.

title: Issue 6 Cover — Brannock Stayed
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 6, “Brannock Stayed.” Keep the iconic Brandon-versus-mural concept, but make the town's adoption of Brannock visibly alive through Tomas and ordinary Last Drop residents.
settingText: Last Drop exterior street and wall in late-afternoon glare: crude community-painted Brannock mural, repairs, water hauling, market/bar activity, people crossing between work and conversation.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: The real Brandon has returned to find that an exaggerated folk version of him has become part of the town's identity.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Slightly low medium-wide composition with the mural filling the upper background and real Brandon in foreground/near-midground, allowing direct visual comparison without making the mural photoreal. Tomas stands nearby clearly alive and improved, interacting with town life. Eva and Jessie react from the side. Several residents use the space normally.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: Brandon's dry discomfort is first read; Tomas's grounded familiarity is second. Residents should show mixed ownership of the Brannock story—fondness, usefulness, argument, indifference—not cult worship. Eva can be fascinated; Jessie can be amused or wary.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: Show how myths get absorbed into ordinary civic life: patched wall, committee table or communal work area without readable paperwork, supplies, local repairs, people greeting Tomas, someone carrying food/water past the mural. The town changed after Brandon left and kept living.
LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Hard late-day gold with chalky wall paint, dust, faded pigments and worn materials. Mural colors should be crude and human-made, not luminous or pristine.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: The mural remains the large graphic device, but its meaning comes from people living beneath it and using the story.
THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, instantly read real Brandon versus oversized painted 'Brannock,' with a populated street proving the legend has social life.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not show the committee asking Brandon to sign as Brannock, Samuel's confirmation, Tomas's public thank-you using Brandon's real name, or the final conclusion.
MUST INCLUDE: Brandon/mural contrast; Tomas visibly alive; working Last Drop community; Eva/Jessie as relational context; crude handmade mural texture.
MUST AVOID: empty street; magical portrait; perfect heroic likeness; propaganda polish; Marcus confrontation; readable political text.

title: Issue 7 Cover — No Names Today
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 7, “No Names Today.” Sell Rowan Hold as a warm, functioning family culture and Nessa as the person whose life is being assigned. Brandon should be visibly unimportant for once.
settingText: Rowan Hold family homestead in active daytime use: shaded yard, food preparation, laundry, ledgers, worktables, repair benches, family movement, an old black Sunforge rib casually incorporated into the landscape.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: Nessa is competent enough that her family has chosen a permanent responsibility for her—while she has already packed to leave.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Medium-wide human-centered composition. Nessa dominates foreground with travel bag and forward-facing posture. Ada stands in the active family space behind/alongside her with ledger keys or responsibility objects, not villainously but firmly. Jessie is a strong secondary presence reading Nessa's situation with personal recognition. Brandon is clearly visible in deep background doing ordinary communal work, receiving no special attention; Eva notices this normality.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: Nessa's mix of capability, affection and refusal is the first read. Ada must look reasonable and loving enough that the dilemma is real. Jessie should visually recognize the trap without hijacking it. Brandon's de-centering is intentional.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: Rowan Hold should be one of the richest lived-community covers: family members preparing food, carrying laundry, maintaining gear, talking across worktables, children/elders if appropriate, goat on or near the inert rib if it fits naturally. Avoid posed ensemble symmetry.

LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Warm open shade with bright Sunfields edges, varied cloth colors, sun-browned wood, paper/ink, food and practical domestic materials. The black rib is inert and almost mundane.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: Packed bag versus ledger/keys is secondary to Nessa and Ada's relationship. The objects clarify the choice; they are not the cover.
THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, Nessa is unmistakable foreground focal figure, with Ada/community mass behind and an open road gap beyond.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not show the family vote, Brandon's consent argument, redistribution of duties, or Nessa's final departure state.
MUST INCLUDE: Nessa as focal character; Ada as credible loving pressure; Jessie as meaningful secondary figure; busy Rowan Hold family life; Brandon de-centered and ordinary.
MUST AVOID: Brandon hero composition; empty-chair metaphor; family as villains; mystery silhouettes; generic farmstead; departure victory pose.

title: Issue 8 Cover — The Farther Rider
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 8, “The Farther Rider.” Preserve the exceptional sparseness of this cover, but make the traveling group itself visually compelling so the Rider feels like an intrusion into people we now know.
settingText: The Long Mile beneath a huge bleached sky: layered pale ridges, hard dry road, wind-cut ground, little vegetation, no settlement clutter.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: The entire uneasy traveling group is together now—and one tiny figure on a distant white ridge refuses to behave like ordinary distance.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Very wide vertical landscape composition with enormous sky, but stage the five travelers as a readable compact foreground/midground cluster rather than anonymous dots. Use different silhouettes: Brandon's dark duster, Eva's small hooded form, Jessie's goggles/utility shape, Raina's polished tracker gear, Samuel's worn preacher layers. Their shared eyeline leads to one tiny Rider high on the ridge.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: The group should show a new, uneasy social arrangement: Raina and Samuel are physically with Brandon/Eva/Jessie, not operating ahead. Their distinct silhouettes and reactions make the reader want to know this strange traveling company. The Rider remains unreadable.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: There is intentionally no local community here; the richness comes from the traveling ensemble itself. Preserve the accumulated differences in costume, age, scale and body language rather than reducing them to generic desert silhouettes.

LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Bleached high light, pale terrain, dark human silhouettes with controlled material detail. No supernatural color cast. Atmospheric perspective must be physically believable.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: Distance is the concept, but the people measuring it with their eyes make the concept emotionally legible.
THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, read as a distinct five-person traveler cluster on the road and one tiny Rider separated by a huge clean field of distance.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not show multiple Rider positions, failed approach geometry, the closer evening appearance, or the morning Rider behind them.
MUST INCLUDE: readable five-person traveling group; one tiny Rider only; credible layered ridge distances; Raina and Samuel visibly traveling with the others.
MUST AVOID: anonymous foreground dots; multiple Riders; glow; portal effects; warped horizon; spectral anatomy; generic posse pose.

title: Issue 9 Cover — Four Quiet Days
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 9, “Four Quiet Days.” Sell Saint Oren as a fascinating community living ordinary lives beneath the largest Sunforge-like structure yet, with Samuel and Alec providing human gravity.
settingText: Saint Oren built beneath and around a massive exposed dark structure: shaded homes, communal eating, repair work, footpaths, people using the shadow as ordinary civic space.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: An astonishing structure hangs over a community where the most important thing happening is an old man, his unfinished relationship, and four ordinary days.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Layered portrait composition. The huge dark structure arcs across the upper third/half, but the human foreground is active and readable. Samuel sits or walks with frail Alec as the strongest emotional pair. Nearby, Brandon is losing at cards or engaged in another ordinary activity; Kayla works through daily hosting. Eva and Raina are present at the edge of this normality, searching for a pattern that refuses to perform.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: Samuel and Alec give the cover heart. Brandon should look ordinary and mildly losing, not mysterious. Kayla grounds the community. Eva/Raina carry observational tension. Avoid making everybody stare at the structure.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: Populate Saint Oren with people cooking, repairing, moving water, working in shade, talking at tables, children or elders crossing the frame if appropriate. The structure should feel incorporated into daily geography rather than worshipped.

LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Broad cool shade under the dark structure with hot bright edges beyond. Skin, food, cards, wood, cloth and ordinary work should hold warm lived color. Structure stays inert, matte and unexplained.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: The visual irony is scale: the giant apparent clue is background architecture while human life remains foreground.
THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, read huge black arc over a warm populated human band, with Samuel/Alec and Brandon's ordinary life still distinct.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not depict Alec's final conversation with his daughter, death imagery, Raina's explicit conclusion, or the departure summary.
MUST INCLUDE: Samuel and Alec as meaningful human pair; Saint Oren community life; Brandon doing something ordinary; Eva/Raina observing; massive inert structure.
MUST AVOID: empty card table as sole hook; structure activation; cult imagery; ominous crowd; deathbed tableau; glow.

title: Issue 10 Cover — The Rookery
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 10, “The Rookery.” This should be one of the richest, coolest covers in the run: a crossroads full of visually distinctive people, including Cadre/Cadre-adjacent energy, while the composition tempts the reader to falsely connect them.
settingText: The Rookery at peak crossroads activity near sunset: converging roads, shade structures, market tables, carts, animals, old dark structural fragments, travelers arriving/leaving, local workers moving between long-established routines.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: The Rookery is full of people so visually distinctive that both Eva and the reader want them to be one mysterious pattern.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Slightly elevated 28–35mm-feeling portrait view looking into a dense crossroads. Eva and Raina occupy a lower-foreground observation axis, both scanning. Marty is a confident central local presence moving through people he actually knows. Dylan Sheets gets a strong visually cool secondary placement with tools/chalk/compass. Brandon, Jessie and Samuel are present but not centered. Arrange at least four or five distinct traveler/local silhouettes across depth so roads, awning poles and eyelines create a tempting false constellation.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: The individual people must be irresistible to inspect: different ages, route cultures, work gear, masks/protective pieces where story-consistent, unusual silhouettes, lived scars, parcels, tools and animals. Marty should visually puncture the mystery by belonging comfortably among them. Dylan should look like someone the reader wants to know more about.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: Make the Rookery feel socially dense rather than chaotic: people owe each other money, carry parcels, repair gear, greet cousins, unload carts, argue over practical things, share shade. Every background action should look independent even though the overall composition seduces the eye into linking them.

LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Low hard Sunfields sun with layered shade, long shadows, warm dust and cooler dark structural fragments. Use selective saturated clothing/material accents on distinctive travelers without collapsing into carnival color.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: The 'constellation' is created entirely by composition—roads, poles, eyelines and spacing—not literal lines, labels or graphics.

THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, read as a compelling crowded crossroads with Eva/Raina scanning and several unusually cool silhouettes distributed through a clear triangular/constellation-like composition.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not explain who is related to whom, reveal the rumor chain, literalize Marty's lesson, or turn the crowd into a confirmed Cadre gathering.
MUST INCLUDE: Marty as grounded local anchor; Dylan as visually magnetic traveler; Eva and Raina pattern-hunting; multiple distinctive independent people; busy lived crossroads culture.
MUST AVOID: generic crowd; literal conspiracy lines; labels; everyone staring at Brandon; mystical assembly; empty crossroads; infographic treatment.

title: Issue 11 Cover — What Jessie Left
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 11, “What Jessie Left.” Sell Jessie and Rachael as two compelling people with a real past. The road remains important, but the human recognition is the reason the image matters.
settingText: Glasshouse courtyard in late-day light: old glass panels, familiar room doors, family/communal supper preparation, travel gear against walls, people moving comfortably through a place Jessie once knew, road visible beyond.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: For once the recognition is correct: somebody knows Jessie Petrescu, knows what she was like here, and is happy/angry enough to say so.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Medium portrait composition with Jessie near the visual hinge between courtyard and road, but Rachael shares the frame strongly rather than appearing as a distant symbol. Rachael can be advancing from a doorway with open expressive body language. Eva is nearby, delighted/curious; Brandon stays peripheral and observant. Populate the Glasshouse behind Rachael with people preparing supper or moving through familiar routines.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: Jessie and Rachael must have immediate relational chemistry: affection, irritation, familiarity, unfinished business. Eva's visible interest adds humor. Brandon's restraint reinforces that this story is Jessie's. Faces and posture are more important than the road.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: Glasshouse should look like a place Jessie really could have lived: familiar cup/storage niches without emphasizing spoiler props, open doors, worn glass, shared food, neighbors/friends, ordinary work. It must feel welcoming enough that leaving was a choice, not escape.
LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Warm late-day light filtered through aged glass, with cooler open-road light beyond. Use reflections and glass texture as atmosphere, not identity trickery.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: The road is a secondary counterweight to a genuinely lived place. The tension comes from a person who knows Jessie, not from abstract choice geometry.
THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, Jessie and Rachael read as the dominant two-person relationship, with Eva as lively secondary and the road/courtyard split clear behind them.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: Do not show the blue cup, state the exact grievance, depict Jessie's confession about staying becoming default, or reveal her decision to stay an extra night.
MUST INCLUDE: Jessie/Rachael chemistry; Eva as curious secondary; Glasshouse community life; visible road as secondary option; Brandon de-centered.
MUST AVOID: Jessie alone against empty road; farewell pose; Brandon-centric cover; generic romantic reunion; showing the stay decision; empty courtyard.

title: Issue 12 Cover — Already Waiting
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 12, “Already Waiting.” Keep the packet as the mystery trigger, but make Maela Crow and the arriving group equally important: this is a promise carried by a real person, not a spooky prop.
settingText: Hushwater weathered household at cool late-day/twilight: visible winter repairs in pale wood, lived kitchen/work space, ordinary textiles and tools, road seen through open doorway.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no generic cast-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.
PRIMARY SELLING IDEA: Maela has been carrying a promise for months; Brandon arrives with both known manipulators beside him, and she still believes the packet belongs to him under another name.

CAMERA / COMPOSITION: Interior-to-doorway portrait composition. Maela is strong foreground/near-midground, one hand near the carefully wrapped packet on the table, body angled toward the arriving group. The packet is sharp but secondary to her face and responsibility. Through the open doorway, Brandon, Raina and Samuel approach together; Eva and Jessie can be visible behind/with them if spatial clarity allows.

HUMAN FOCAL HIERARCHY: Maela must look tired, stubbornly responsible and immediately real—the kind of person who would keep a promise through winter. Brandon's polite caution is the second read. Raina and Samuel being visibly present at the same arrival is crucial because their bodies in the frame make the mystery logically sharper. Eva/Jessie provide accumulated group continuity.

COMMUNITY / WORLD RICHNESS: Hushwater should look inhabited rather than gothic: repaired boards, practical household table, worn cloth, tools, cooking/storage, neighboring structures glimpsed outside. This is a normal house that has held an abnormal expectation.
LIGHT / PALETTE / MATERIALS: Cool exterior twilight against warmer interior household light. Winter-repair pale wood and cloth packet should be tactile; no eerie color effects.
SYMBOLIC SUPPORT: The packet concentrates the mystery, but Maela's promise and the group's simultaneous arrival make it meaningful.
THUMBNAIL READ: At small size, read Maela + packet in foreground and the unmistakable Brandon/Raina/Samuel trio framed together in the doorway behind.

TRADE-DRESS ZONE: Preserve the established Issue 1 masthead and cover-brand architecture. Keep the upper masthead area readable and uncluttered; do not place a key face, hand, or central story object where the logo must cover it.
SPOILER CEILING: No readable name, no Andrew Keane label, no ledger date, no dying-friend explanation, no proof of when the traveler came, no packet opening, no resolution.
MUST INCLUDE: Maela as full human focal character; packet as secondary mystery object; Brandon/Raina/Samuel arriving together; Eva/Jessie if composition remains clear; ordinary lived Hushwater home.
MUST AVOID: packet-only still life; mystical glow; Rider cameo; timeline graphic; readable label; gothic haunted-house treatment; showing contents.
